extracted_claims.text: Annex III, point 4 of the EU AI Act lists AI systems intended for recruitment (e.g., CV-sorting, candidate screening) as high-risk.

Under Article 26, deployers of high-risk AI systems must use the system according to the provider's instructions, ensure competent human oversight, monitor the system's operation, manage input data, keep automatically generated logs for at least six months, and inform the provider or relevant authorities of risks or serious incidents.
Under Article 26, deployers must notify workers' representatives and affected workers before or when a high-risk AI system is used in the workplace.
Article 26 requires deployers to ensure staff operating the high-risk AI system have sufficient training/AI literacy; relying solely on the provider's instructions for use is not sufficient.
Under Article 27, deployers of certain high-risk AI systems must conduct a fundamental rights impact assessment prior to the system's first use, and update it if circumstances change.
Deployers of high-risk AI systems listed in Annex III that make or assist in decisions about natural persons must inform those individuals that they are subject to the AI system (Article 26(11)).
Under Article 13, providers of high-risk AI systems must design systems to be sufficiently transparent and must supply deployers with instructions for use in an appropriate digital or other format.
Providers (not deployers) of high-risk AI systems must implement a risk management system (Article 9) and data and data governance measures (Article 10).
Public authorities deploying high-risk AI systems must comply with a registration obligation, including registering in the EU database for high-risk AI systems listed in Annex III (Article 71).

Two prohibited AI practices under the AI Act are directly relevant to hiring: use of emotion-recognition AI during recruitment, and biometric categorization inferring protected traits such as race, political opinion, or religion; both bans have applied since 2 February 2025.

Fines for violating prohibited AI practices can reach up to €35 million or 7% of global turnover; other high-risk-related violations carry lower maximum fines (reported as up to €15 million in one source).
National market surveillance authorities are responsible for most compliance investigations and enforcement of the AI Act, while the EU AI Office enforces obligations for general-purpose AI models.
Member States were required to adopt and notify the Commission of national penalty rules (including administrative fines) by 2 August 2025.
As of June 2026, no public EU AI Act penalties had been issued.

In February 2026, the U.S. DOJ settled with Elegant Enterprise-Wide Solutions Inc. over AI-generated job advertisements containing unauthorized visa-status restrictions; this is a U.S. enforcement action under U.S. law, not the EU AI Act.

In April 2026, a U.S. federal court (in xAI v. Weiser) enjoined enforcement of the Colorado Artificial Intelligence Act pending further proceedings; this is a U.S. state-law enforcement development, not EU-based.

Texas's TRAIGA law bans intentional AI-based discrimination in hiring but rejects disparate impact as a standalone basis for liability, with the state attorney general holding exclusive enforcement power and a mandatory 60-day cure period before penalties; this is U.S. state law, not EU law.
Italy's national AI Law (Law No. 132/2025), effective 10 October 2025, establishes national-level fines up to €774,685 for violations under Italian law, supplementing the EU AI Act framework.

In late 2025 the European Commission proposed a 'Digital Omnibus' package that could postpone certain Annex III high-risk obligations until December 2027; as of March 2026 this proposal had not been adopted.

report:
# Compliance Requirements and Enforcement for High-Risk AI Hiring Tools Under the EU AI Act

## Executive Summary
AI recruitment tools (CV-sorting, candidate screening) are classified as high-risk under Annex III of the EU AI Act, triggering substantial obligations for both providers and deployers (high confidence) ([Futurium](https://futurium.ec.europa.eu/en/apply-ai-alliance/community-content/office-has-become-diy-ai-lab-who-checking-what-goes-and-what-comes-out), [Recruitly](https://recruitly.io/resources/ai-act-for-recruiters)). Core Article 26 obligations—human oversight, system monitoring, and logging—are supported with high confidence ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-26)), while related duties such as worker notification and fundamental rights impact assessments are supported with medium confidence. Significant uncertainty surrounds the exact compliance deadlines—ranging from August 2027 to December 2027—and as of mid-2026 no public EU AI Act penalties had been issued, though it remains unconfirmed whether any enforcement action has specifically targeted a hiring tool deployer (low confidence).

## Key Findings

### Classification and Core Obligations
AI systems used for recruitment, including CV-sorting and candidate screening, are designated high-risk under Annex III, point 4 of the EU AI Act (high confidence) ([Futurium](https://futurium.ec.europa.eu/en/apply-ai-alliance/community-content/office-has-become-diy-ai-lab-who-checking-what-goes-and-what-comes-out), [Recruitly](https://recruitly.io/resources/ai-act-for-recruiters)). Under Article 26, deployers must use systems per provider instructions, ensure competent human oversight, monitor operation, manage input data, retain automatically generated logs for at least six months, and report risks or serious incidents (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-26), [EDPB](https://www.edpb.europa.eu/system/files/2025-06/spe-training-on-ai-and-data-protection-legal_en.pdf)).

### Worker and Candidate Rights
Deployers must notify workers' representatives and affected employees before or when a high-risk AI system is deployed in the workplace (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-26)). Individuals subject to high-risk AI-assisted decisions must be informed that an AI system is involved, per Article 26(11) (high confidence) ([EUR-Lex](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML?uri=CELEX%3A02024R1689-20260727)).

### Staff Training and Impact Assessments
Deployers must ensure staff operating these systems have sufficient AI literacy and training, beyond merely following provider instructions (medium confidence) ([Digital Strategy](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/faqs/ai-literacy-questions-answers)). Article 27 requires certain deployers to conduct a fundamental rights impact assessment before first use, updated as circumstances change (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-27)).

### Provider Obligations
Providers—not deployers—must implement risk management systems (Article 9) and data governance measures (Article 10), and supply transparent instructions for use (Article 13) (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk, Art. 9](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-9), [Art. 13](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-13)). Public-sector deployers face additional registration obligations in the EU database (medium confidence) ([Article 71](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-71)).

### Prohibited Practices
Two prohibited practices are directly relevant to hiring—emotion-recognition AI in recruitment and biometric categorization inferring protected traits—both banned since 2 February 2025, though this claim rests on a single source (low confidence) ([Metaview](https://www.metaview.ai/resources/blog/ai-hiring-laws-2026-2027)).

### Enforcement and Penalties
Violations of prohibited practices can trigger fines up to €35 million or 7% of global turnover, with other high-risk violations carrying lower maxima, reportedly up to €15 million (medium confidence) ([Recruitly](https://recruitly.io/resources/ai-act-for-recruiters), [DLA Piper](https://intelligence.dlapiper.com/artificial-intelligence?t=08-enforcement&c=EU)). National market surveillance authorities handle most enforcement, while the EU AI Office oversees general-purpose AI models (low confidence) ([Jaggaer](https://www.jaggaer.com/blog/eu-ai-act-fines-penalties), [Orrick](https://www.orrick.com/en/Insights/2024/09/The-EU-AI-Act-Oversight-and-Enforcement)). Member States were required to notify national penalty rules by 2 August 2025 (medium confidence) ([DLA Piper](https://intelligence.dlapiper.com/artificial-intelligence?t=08-enforcement&c=EU)). As of June 2026, no public EU AI Act penalties had been issued (low confidence) ([Jaggaer](https://www.jaggaer.com/blog/eu-ai-act-fines-penalties)); no source confirms whether this absence specifically covers hiring tool deployers, so a hiring-specific enforcement gap cannot be ruled in or out. Italy's national Law 132/2025 adds supplementary fines up to €774,685 (low confidence) ([Orbiqhq](https://www.orbiqhq.com/eu-regulations/eu-ai-act-compliance)).

## Contradictions & Uncertainties
Sources conflict on when Annex III high-risk obligations for hiring AI take effect: 2 August 2027 versus 2 December 2027 ([Recruitly](https://recruitly.io/resources/ai-act-for-recruiters) vs. [Jaggaer](https://www.jaggaer.com/blog/eu-ai-act-fines-penalties)). GPAI obligation/penalty dates also diverge by a year ([Jaggaer](https://www.jaggaer.com/blog/eu-ai-act-fines-penalties) vs. [Orrick](https://www.orrick.com/en/Insights/2024/09/The-EU-AI-Act-Oversight-and-Enforcement), latter flagged low confidence at 0.10). Whether the "Digital Omnibus" delay proposal has been adopted is contested: one source says it remained pending as of March 2026 ([Orbiqhq](https://www.orbiqhq.com/eu-regulations/eu-ai-act-compliance), low confidence), while the EUR-Lex consolidated text dated July 2026 appears to incorporate its amendments ([EUR-Lex](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML?uri=CELEX%3A02024R1689-20260727)). Several low-confidence claims (0.10–0.17) concerning U.S. enforcement actions (DOJ settlement, Colorado AIA injunction, Texas TRAIGA) are not EU AI Act actions and should not be conflated with EU enforcement. The prohibited-practices claim, the national-authority enforcement claim, and the "no penalties issued" claim are all flagged below the 0.4 confidence threshold and should be treated cautiously.

## Knowledge Gaps
It remains unclear whether the Digital Omnibus delay has been formally adopted and what the definitive compliance deadline is. No confirmed EU enforcement action against a specific high-risk hiring AI tool has been identified; this absence is itself a gap rather than evidence that none has occurred. Practical documentation standards for Article 27 assessments, interaction with GDPR/labor law enforcement, and EU AI Office guidance specific to recruitment AI remain undetermined.

## Methodology Note
This report was produced by an automated research pipeline: web search, source classification, confidence scores computed from source authority, recency and corroboration, and an automated review against the extracted claims.

source_links.notes: Every link points to a gathered source.

citation_coverage.notes: Nearly all factual statements carry inline markdown citations. The executive summary's claim 'as of mid-2026 no public EU AI Act penalties had been issued, though it remains unconfirmed whether any enforcement action has specifically targeted a hiring tool deployer' lacks its own citation, but it restates a claim that is cited later in the body (Jaggaer), so this is a minor stylistic issue rather than a coverage failure.

hallucination_check.notes: Checked numeric and date claims (€35M/7%, €15M, €774,685, 2 Feb 2025 ban, 2 Aug 2025 notification deadline, Art. 26/27 obligations, Annex III classification) against the extracted claims and all match the source claims with appropriate confidence labeling. No fabricated facts or numbers were found that are absent from the claim set.

contradiction_disclosure.notes: The report explicitly surfaces the August 2027 vs December 2027 Annex III deadline conflict, the GPAI date discrepancy, and the disputed status of the Digital Omnibus adoption, matching the 'Known Contradictions' list. It also appropriately warns that US enforcement actions (DOJ, Colorado, Texas) should not be conflated with EU AI Act enforcement.

confidence_assessment.notes: Confidence labels attached to each claim in the report (e.g., Art. 26 'high confidence', worker notification 'medium confidence', prohibited practices and enforcement claims 'low confidence') align closely with the underlying claim confidence scores (0.82, 0.68, 0.12-0.17 respectively).

executive_summary_accuracy.notes: The executive summary's statements about high-risk classification, Article 26 obligations, deadline uncertainty, and absence of confirmed penalties accurately reflect the detailed findings and contradictions discussed in the body.

knowledge_gaps.notes: The Knowledge Gaps section clearly lists the Digital Omnibus adoption uncertainty, absence of confirmed hiring-specific enforcement action, undetermined Article 27 documentation standards, and the GDPR/labor law interplay, consistent with the 'Open Issues' in the ground truth.
